After a restart the phone stays encrypted until you unlock it for the first time. Android calls that Direct Boot, and most apps cannot run at all until then. This one can: its lists and its settings are kept where they can be read before unlocking, so calls are screened even right after a restart.

What it cannot read in that time are your contacts - they stay locked away until the phone is unlocked, so a call from a contact looks like a call from a stranger. The setting below decides which kinds of blocking are allowed until then: a kind you switch off here lets those calls through until you unlock the phone.
Allowed kinds of blocking in Direct Boot mode (Contacts can\'t be reliably used as a whitelist in this mode)

Country codes are used in requests to 3rd party servers. These codes are set to mimic the behavior of the official 3rd party app. If the codes match your real country (may be detected by your IP address) then your requests will look the most inconspicuous. Auto-detection is used by default (based on mobile network information or system locale), which should be fine for most users, but you can set the codes manually. The database holds numbers from everywhere. Filtering keeps the ones that can reach you and drops the rest, which saves storage; nothing else about the app changes. It happens while the database is fetched and after every update. Every source is compiled into one table first and a copy of it is put aside; the filter then runs on that table, so filtering always starts from the unfiltered database - and when no copy is kept, the sources are asked for it again rather than a narrowed database being narrowed further

Enter the number in +COUNTRY-NUMBER format (as Android would show in your dialer). Three things can stand in for digits: \"*\" for any digits or none, \"#\" for exactly one digit, and \"{30,40}\" for one of several alternatives. For example, +49{30,40}* covers every number starting with +4930 or +4940, and +49301234## covers the hundred numbers of that extension range. The form the number was dialled or logged in does not matter: an entry written as +49221472585 also covers a call logged as 0221472585.

A service for monitoring phone state in background

The app knows nothing about a number by itself: everything comes from the sources you list, in the order you put them in.

• No source is "the database" and the rest additions to it: every source can hand over a whole one, and the order alone decides. The first source fills the empty table; every source after it changes what it knows about, leaves the rest alone, and can also take numbers out again.
• The number is the key of the table, so a number several sources know is one entry. The later source changes the fields it has something to say about; the others stay as they were.
• A build works on a database of its own, beside the one in use. Only when it is whole does it take the place of the old one – so a build that fails leaves what worked untouched, and lookups never see a half-built database.
• Only numbers matching the pattern you set are written down at all – the rest are skipped as the sources are read, so the database never holds nine million numbers to delete most of them again. Changing the pattern means building again, which needs no download.
• The first source's files are the ones the library keeps, and they are only downloaded when there are none, when you point the source somewhere else, or when its own schedule says so – it is tens of megabytes. "Fetch now" on a source fetches it whatever that says.
• A number is looked up in that table and not in the downloaded files, so every source counts, whatever it handed over – and a number a later source took out stays out. What the app fetches between builds goes straight into the table as well.
• What each build did, source by source, is in the build log under Database.

Some things say "let it through" and some say "block it", and they are not asked in the order they are listed in the settings.

Allowed, whatever anything else says:
• the number is in your contacts
• the number is on your whitelist
• the number is on the allow list of your PhoneBlock account

Nothing below is consulted then – a call from a contact is never blocked.

Otherwise it is blocked by the first of these that applies (each only if you switched it on):
1. the number is withheld
2. the community database rates it negative
3. it is on your blacklist
4. PhoneBlock has it as spam, or it is on the block list of your account

On Android 11 and newer, a call the network says is not coming from the number it claims is blocked before any of this, if you switched that on.

When the phone has not been unlocked since it was started, your contacts and lists can't be read. What may still block then is a setting of its own in the advanced settings.

• A number is matched in every form it can be written in: +4930123456, 004930123456 and 030123456 are the same number, and an entry in any of those forms finds it.
• An entry can be a pattern rather than a number – 49* covers every German number – and the app shows which entry matched, so a call blocked by a pattern says which pattern it was.
• Putting a number on one list takes it off the other.
• The whitelist wins over the blacklist, and contacts win over both.

What this app knows about a number it did not find out itself. The ratings and the reviews come from the Should I Answer community database; a PhoneBlock account adds what that community has collected; lists such as tellows can be added as sources of their own. Behind all of it are people writing down who called them.
